title: Genetics and Heredity: DNA, Genes, Punnett Squares, and Mutations
objectives: Students will describe the relationship among DNA, genes, and chromosomes and use base-pairing rules to write a complementary DNA strand.
Students will use the terms allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, and heterozygous correctly.
Students will complete Punnett squares and use them to find the probability of a trait and the expected number of offspring with that trait.
Students will recognize incomplete dominance and codominance and explain how they change the expected results of a cross.
Students will identify types of mutations, explain their possible effects, and determine whether a mutation can be inherited.
teach:
Week 5 Science: Genetics and Heredity — DNA, Genes, Chromosomes, Traits, Punnett Squares, and Mutations

Objectives

  • Describe how DNA, genes, and chromosomes are related, and write a complementary DNA strand using base-pairing rules.
  • Use allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, and heterozygous correctly.
  • Complete a Punnett square and use it to state a probability (as a fraction, a percent, and a ratio) and an expected number of offspring.
  • Recognize incomplete dominance and codominance.
  • Identify substitution, insertion, and deletion mutations, describe possible effects, and decide whether a mutation can be passed to children.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors (one color for each parent's alleles).
  • Two coins for each student or pair (for the probability demonstration).
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Blank 2 × 2 grids for Punnett squares (students can draw their own).
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5The brown-eyed parents puzzle and a two-coin probability question.
Direct instruction20DNA, genes, chromosomes; alleles and the vocabulary of inheritance; Punnett squares, probability, and expected numbers; other inheritance patterns; mutations. Worked Examples 1–4.
Guided practice15Four problems worked with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket and study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Pose two questions and give students one minute each to discuss with a partner.

  1. Two parents both have brown eyes. Their daughter has blue eyes. How is that possible?
  2. You flip two coins at the same time. What is the chance that both land tails up?

Answers: (1) Each parent can carry a hidden instruction for blue eyes that is covered up by the instruction for brown eyes. If each parent passes the hidden instruction to the daughter, she shows blue eyes. (Eye color is actually controlled by several genes, but this simple model is the right idea for today.) (2) The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Only one is “both tails,” so the chance is 1 out of 4, or 1/4 = 25%.

Bridge: Tell students that by the end of the lesson they will see that question 1 and question 2 are really the same math. Parents pass on alleles the way coins land: by chance.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. DNA is the instruction molecule. Every living cell contains DNA. Its shape is a double helix, like a twisted ladder. Each rung of the ladder is a pair of bases. There are four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G). The pairing rule never changes: A pairs with T and C pairs with G. The order of bases along one side is the code, just as the order of letters in a sentence carries its meaning.

2. Genes and chromosomes. A gene is a section of DNA that holds the instructions for making one protein. Proteins build and run the body, so genes affect traits such as blood type or the ability to digest milk. A chromosome is one very long DNA molecule, tightly coiled, that carries hundreds to thousands of genes. Draw the size ladder on the board:

base < gene < chromosome < nucleus < cell

Human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. One chromosome of each pair came from the mother and one from the father. Sex cells (egg and sperm) carry only 23, one from each pair, so a fertilized egg ends up with 46 again.

3. Alleles and the vocabulary of inheritance. Because chromosomes come in pairs, a person has two copies of most genes. Different versions of the same gene are called alleles. Write the key terms and an example of each:

  • Dominant allele: shows its trait whenever it is present; written with a capital letter (T = tall pea plant).
  • Recessive allele: shows its trait only when there are two copies; written with the lowercase of the same letter (t = short).
  • Genotype: the pair of alleles (TT, Tt, or tt). Phenotype: the trait you can observe (tall or short).
  • Homozygous: two identical alleles (TT is homozygous dominant; tt is homozygous recessive). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Tt). A heterozygous person with a recessive disease allele is called a carrier.

Stress that “dominant” does not mean “more common” or “stronger.” It only describes which allele shows up in a heterozygous individual.

4. Punnett squares, probability, and expected numbers. Teach the four steps, using one marker color per parent:

  1. Write each parent's genotype.
  2. Split each genotype into its two alleles. Put one parent's alleles across the top and the other parent's down the side.
  3. Fill each box with one allele from its column and one from its row. Write the capital letter first.
  4. Count. Each of the four boxes is an equally likely outcome, so each box = 1/4 = 25%.

Then connect to the math students already know from Week 2: expected number = probability × total number of offspring. Real results come close to the expected numbers but rarely match exactly, just as 100 coin flips rarely give exactly 50 heads. Also stress that each offspring is a separate event: the chances are the same for every child, no matter what happened with earlier children.

5. Not every trait follows the simple dominant/recessive pattern. In incomplete dominance, the heterozygous individual shows a blend: red (RR) snapdragons crossed with white (WW) snapdragons produce pink (RW) flowers. In codominance, both alleles show fully: a person with type AB blood makes both A and B markers. Many traits, such as height and skin color, are controlled by many genes plus the environment (nutrition, sunlight), so they do not follow a single Punnett square.

6. Mutations. A mutation is a change in the base sequence of DNA. Three types to know:

  • Substitution: one base is replaced by another. It may change one amino acid in the protein, or none at all.
  • Insertion: an extra base is added.
  • Deletion: a base is removed. Insertions and deletions shift how the rest of the gene is read, so they often change many amino acids.

Mutations can happen from copying errors when a cell divides or from mutagens such as ultraviolet light, X-rays, tobacco smoke, and certain chemicals. Effects can be harmful, neutral, or helpful. The key heredity rule: only mutations in sex cells (egg or sperm) can be passed to children. A mutation in a skin or lung cell can affect that person (for example, by contributing to cancer) but is not inherited.

Worked Example 1: A cross between two heterozygous plants

In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be short? If the cross produces 400 seeds, how many are expected to grow into short plants?

Tt
TTTTt
tTttt

Genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Phenotypes: 3 tall (TT, Tt, Tt) : 1 short (tt).

Probability of short = 1/4 = 25%.

Expected number short = 1/4 × 400 = 100 plants. (Expected tall = 3/4 × 400 = 300.)

Worked Example 2: The test cross

In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant over white fur (b). A breeder has a black guinea pig and does not know whether it is BB or Bb. She crosses it with a white guinea pig (bb). What results would tell her the genotype?

If the black parent is BB: every box is Bb, so 100% of the pups are black.

Bb
bBbbb
bBbbb

If the black parent is Bb (square above): 2 Bb : 2 bb, so 50% black and 50% white.

Conclusion: if even one white pup appears, the black parent must be Bb, because a white pup (bb) needs a b allele from each parent. In a litter of 12 from a Bb × bb cross, the expected number of white pups is 1/2 × 12 = 6.

Worked Example 3: Base pairing and a mutation

One strand of a DNA segment reads T A C G G A T T C. (a) Write the complementary strand. (b) A mutation changes the strand to T A C A G A T T C. What type of mutation is this? (c) What if the strand had become T A C G A T T C?

(a) Pair each base: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→T, T→A, T→A, C→G. Complement: A T G C C T A A G.

(b) Compare base by base: the 4th base changed from G to A, and the strand is still 9 bases long. One base was swapped, so this is a substitution.

(c) The new strand has 8 bases; one of the two Gs (positions 4 and 5) is missing. This is a deletion. Read in groups of three, the original TAC GGA TTC becomes TAC GAT TC…, so every group after the deletion is different. That is why deletions and insertions usually do more damage than a single substitution.

Worked Example 4: Carriers of a recessive disorder

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two parents are both carriers (Ff). What is the probability that a child has cystic fibrosis? That a child is a carrier? If their first three children do not have the disorder, what is the chance the fourth child has it?

Ff
FFFFf
fFfff

Has the disorder (ff): 1 box of 4 = 1/4 = 25%.

Carrier (Ff): 2 boxes of 4 = 2/4 = 50%.

Fourth child: still 25%. Each child is a separate event; earlier children do not change the odds.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Students work each problem on paper; call on volunteers to show the Punnett square or reasoning before revealing the answer.

  1. In pea plants, round seeds (R) are dominant over wrinkled seeds (r). Cross Rr × rr. What percent of offspring are expected to have wrinkled seeds? Out of 60 seeds, how many are expected to be wrinkled?
  2. Write the complementary strand for G G A T C A.
  3. A pink snapdragon (RW) is crossed with a white snapdragon (WW). What are the expected phenotypes and percents?
  4. A worker's skin cells develop a mutation after years of sun exposure. Can the mutation be passed to the worker's children? Explain.

Answers: (1) Boxes: Rr, Rr, rr, rr. Wrinkled = 2/4 = 50%. Expected wrinkled = 0.50 × 60 = 30 seeds. (2) C C T A G T. (3) Boxes: RW, RW, WW, WW. 50% pink, 50% white (no red, because there is no way to get RR). (4) No. Skin cells are body cells, not sex cells, so the change is not in any egg or sperm. Only mutations in sex cells are inherited.

Checks for Understanding

  • “What is the difference between a genotype and a phenotype?” Expected: the genotype is the pair of alleles (such as Tt); the phenotype is the observable trait (tall).
  • “Can two short (tt) pea plants have a tall offspring?” Expected: no; neither parent has a T allele to pass on, so every offspring is tt (barring a rare new mutation).
  • “A Punnett square shows 3/4 purple. Out of 80 offspring, how many are expected to be purple?” Expected: 3/4 × 80 = 60.
  • “Which kind of mutation shifts the reading of every base after it?” Expected: an insertion or a deletion.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

  • Putting both of one parent's alleles on the same box. Each box gets exactly one allele from the top and one from the side. Have students trace with two colors to check.
  • Thinking “dominant” means “more common.” Some dominant alleles are rare (for example, the allele for having extra fingers). Dominance only describes what shows up in a heterozygous individual.
  • Reading a 3 : 1 ratio as 3/1 or as 1/3. A 3 : 1 ratio means 3 out of every 4 total, so the fraction is 3/4 (75%). Always add the parts of a ratio to get the total.
  • Answering with the probability when the question asks for a number. If the question says “how many of 200 offspring,” multiply: probability × 200.
  • The “due for it” error. Students may think that after three healthy children the fourth is more likely to be affected. The probability is the same for every child.
  • Assuming every mutation is harmful. Many are neutral, and some are helpful in certain environments.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a pre-drawn Punnett square with the parent alleles already placed, and a fill-in sentence frame: “___ out of 4 boxes show ___, so the probability is ___%.” Let students use the two-coin model (heads = dominant allele, tails = recessive) to simulate 20 offspring from Tt × Tt and compare their count with the expected 15 : 5.

Stretch: Ask students to work backward: “A cross produced 48 offspring, 36 with the dominant trait and 12 with the recessive trait. What were the likely parent genotypes?” (36 : 12 = 3 : 1, so both parents are heterozygous.) Then ask why a 26 : 22 split from a dominant × recessive cross points to a heterozygous parent (close to 1 : 1).

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Punnett square questions give a short description of a trait and a cross, sometimes with a partly completed square, then ask for a probability (“What is the probability that an offspring will have white flowers?”) or an expected number (“how many of the 120 offspring are expected to…”). Answers may appear as fractions, percents, or ratios, or the item may ask the student to type a number.
  • Working backward from data: a table of offspring counts and the question “Which parent genotypes are most likely?”
  • Reading passages about a genetic disorder or a mutation, followed by questions such as “Which statement is supported by the passage?” or “Select two…” items.
  • Drop-down and drag-and-drop items asking students to complete a sentence with the correct term (genotype, phenotype, heterozygous) or sort genotypes into categories.
  • The GED provides the details of the trait in each question; students are not expected to memorize which human traits are dominant.
student:
Genetics and Heredity: How Traits Pass from Parents to Children

Why do children often look like their parents, and how can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child? The answers come from genetics, the study of how traits are inherited. On the GED Science test you will read about crosses, fill in or read Punnett squares, and calculate probabilities. The math is simple once you learn the routine.

1. DNA, genes, and chromosomes

DNA is the molecule that carries the instructions for building and running a living thing. It is shaped like a twisted ladder called a double helix. Each rung is a pair of bases. There are four bases, and they always pair the same way:

A pairs with T. C pairs with G.

A gene is a section of DNA with the instructions for one protein. Proteins do most of the work in your body, so genes shape your traits. A chromosome is one long, tightly coiled DNA molecule that holds many genes. From smallest to largest: base, gene, chromosome, nucleus, cell.

Human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. You got one chromosome of each pair from your mother and one from your father. Egg and sperm cells carry only 23, one from each pair.

2. Alleles: two copies of each gene

Because chromosomes come in pairs, you have two copies of most genes. The different versions of a gene are called alleles.

  • A dominant allele shows its trait whenever it is present. It is written with a capital letter: T for tall.
  • A recessive allele shows its trait only when there are two copies. It is written with the lowercase letter: t for short.
Genotype (alleles)NamePhenotype (what you see)
TTHomozygous dominantTall
TtHeterozygousTall
ttHomozygous recessiveShort

The genotype is the pair of letters. The phenotype is the trait you can observe. Notice that TT and Tt look the same. A heterozygous person who has one allele for a recessive disorder but does not have the disorder is called a carrier.

3. Punnett squares in four steps

  1. Write each parent's genotype.
  2. Put one parent's two alleles across the top and the other parent's down the side.
  3. Fill each box with one letter from the top and one from the side. Write the capital letter first.
  4. Count the boxes. Each box is 1 out of 4, or 25%.

To find how many offspring you should expect, multiply:

Expected number = probability × total number of offspring

Example 1. In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white flowers (p). Cross Pp × Pp. What is the probability of white flowers? Out of 120 seeds, how many are expected to have purple flowers?

Pp
PPPPp
pPppp

White (pp): 1 box out of 4 = 1/4 = 25%.

Purple (PP, Pp, Pp): 3 boxes out of 4 = 3/4 = 75%.

Expected purple: 3/4 × 120 = 90 seeds. The ratio is 3 purple : 1 white.

Example 2. Cross Pp × pp. What percent of the offspring are expected to be white?

Pp
pPppp
pPppp

White (pp): 2 boxes out of 4 = 2/4 = 50%. The ratio is 1 purple : 1 white.

Remember: each offspring is a new event. If two carriers have three healthy children, the chance that the fourth child has the disorder is still 25%. Also, real results are close to the expected numbers but usually not exact.

4. When the pattern is different

Some traits do not follow the simple dominant/recessive rule.

  • Incomplete dominance: the heterozygous offspring shows a blend. Red snapdragons (RR) crossed with white snapdragons (WW) give pink flowers (RW).
  • Codominance: both alleles show fully. A person with type AB blood shows both the A and the B markers.
  • Many traits, such as height, are controlled by several genes and by the environment.

5. Mutations

A mutation is a change in the order of bases in DNA.

  • Substitution: one base is swapped for another. (TAC GGA becomes TAC AGA.)
  • Insertion: an extra base is added.
  • Deletion: a base is removed.

Insertions and deletions change how every base after them is read, so they usually change the protein a lot. Mutations can come from copying mistakes or from things like ultraviolet light, X-rays, and tobacco smoke. A mutation can be harmful, neutral, or helpful. Only mutations in egg or sperm cells can be passed to children.

Example 3. A DNA strand reads C A T G A C. Write its complementary strand.

Pair each base: C→G, A→T, T→A, G→C, A→T, C→G.

Complementary strand: G T A C T G.

Watch out: When a ratio is 3 : 1, the fraction is 3/4, not 3/1. Add the parts (3 + 1 = 4) to get the total. And when a question asks “how many,” give a number, not a percent.

Try It

1. Write the complementary strand for A A G C T T.

Show answer

A→T, A→T, G→C, C→G, T→A, T→A. Answer: T T C G A A.

2. In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant over white fur (b). What is the phenotype of a guinea pig with genotype Bb? Is it homozygous or heterozygous?

Show answer

Black fur, because the dominant B allele is present. It is heterozygous because its two alleles are different.

3. Cross Tt × tt in pea plants (T = tall, t = short). What is the probability of a short plant?

Show answer

Boxes: Tt, Tt, tt, tt. Short (tt) = 2/4 = 1/2 = 50%.

4. Two carriers of a recessive disorder (Ff × Ff) have 8 children in a large family study. How many of the 8 are expected to have the disorder?

Show answer

Probability of ff = 1/4. Expected number = 1/4 × 8 = 2 children.

5. The strand G C A T T A changes to G C A A T T A. What type of mutation is this?

Show answer

The new strand has 7 bases instead of 6; an extra A was added after the third base. This is an insertion.
post:
Post Lesson: Genetics and Heredity

Summary of Key Points

  • DNA is a double helix of paired bases: A with T, C with G. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. A chromosome is a long coiled DNA molecule with many genes. Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
  • You have two alleles for most genes, one from each parent. A dominant allele (capital letter) shows whenever it is present; a recessive allele (lowercase) shows only with two copies.
  • Genotype = the letters (Tt). Phenotype = the trait you see (tall). Homozygous = same alleles; heterozygous = different alleles.
  • In a Punnett square, each box is 1/4 = 25%. Expected number = probability × total offspring.
  • Incomplete dominance blends traits (pink snapdragons); codominance shows both (AB blood).
  • Mutations (substitution, insertion, deletion) change the DNA sequence. Only mutations in egg or sperm cells are inherited.

Exit Ticket

1. Which is larger: a gene or a chromosome?

Show answer

A chromosome. One chromosome carries many genes.

2. Write the complementary strand for T G C A.

Show answer

A C G T

3. In pea plants, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant over green seeds (y). Cross Yy × Yy. What percent of offspring are expected to have green seeds?

Show answer

Boxes: YY, Yy, Yy, yy. Green (yy) = 1/4 = 25%.

4. Using the cross in question 3, how many of 200 offspring are expected to have yellow seeds?

Show answer

Yellow = 3/4. Expected = 3/4 × 200 = 150.

5. A mutation happens in a cell in a person's liver. Can it be inherited by the person's children?

Show answer

No. Liver cells are body cells. Only mutations in egg or sperm cells are passed to children.

Reflection

  • Explain to a friend, in your own words, how two parents who do not show a trait can have a child who does.
  • Which step of the Punnett square method do you need to slow down on? What will you do to check it?
  • Why do you think real offspring counts are close to, but not exactly the same as, the expected numbers?

This Week's Study Plan (20–40 minutes a day)

DayWhat to do
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Make flash cards for the vocabulary terms. Do the Try It problems without looking at the answers.
Day 2DNA and mutations: write three DNA strands of your own and their complements. Change each one by a substitution, an insertion, or a deletion and label the type. Do practice items 1–4.
Day 3Punnett squares: draw squares for TT × tt, Tt × Tt, and Tt × tt. For each, write the probability of the recessive trait and the expected number out of 100. Do practice items 5–8.
Day 4Do practice items 9–12. Review any items you missed and reread their explanations.
Day 5Take this week's Practice GED in one sitting with the timer on.
Day 6Review every Practice GED question you missed. Write one sentence for each explaining the correct answer. Reread the Study Notes.

Test-Taking Strategy: Draw the Square, Even When It Looks Easy

Genetics questions are quick points if you draw the Punnett square on your scratch paper every time. It takes about 20 seconds, and it prevents the most common errors, such as reading 3 : 1 as 1/3 or forgetting that a heterozygous parent can pass on a recessive allele. After drawing it, reread the last line of the question: does it ask for a percent, a ratio, a genotype, a phenotype, or a number of offspring? Then answer exactly that.

Study Notes: Genetics and Heredity

DNA Basics

  • Double helix; four bases.
  • A–T and C–G.
  • base < gene < chromosome < nucleus < cell
  • Gene = instructions for one protein.
  • Humans: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); egg and sperm: 23.

Punnett Square Steps

  1. Write both parent genotypes.
  2. One parent across the top, one down the side.
  3. Each box: one letter from top + one from side.
  4. Count: each box = 1/4 = 25%.

Expected number = probability × total

Ratio 3 : 1 means 3/4 and 1/4 (add the parts).

Key Terms

  • Allele: one version of a gene.
  • Dominant (T) shows if present; recessive (t) needs two copies.
  • Genotype = letters; phenotype = trait seen.
  • Homozygous: TT or tt. Heterozygous: Tt.
  • Carrier: heterozygous for a recessive disorder.
  • Incomplete dominance: blend (RW = pink).
  • Codominance: both show (AB blood).

Mutations

  • Substitution: one base swapped.
  • Insertion: base added. Deletion: base removed (both shift the reading).
  • Causes: copying errors, UV light, X-rays, smoke, chemicals.
  • Harmful, neutral, or helpful.
  • Inherited only if in egg or sperm.

stimuli.title: Flower Color in Pea Plants
stimuli.html:
Pea plants have been used to study heredity for more than 150 years because they grow quickly, produce many seeds, and show traits that are easy to see. In pea plants, one gene controls flower color. The gene has two alleles: the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant, and the allele for white flowers (p) is recessive.

A plant breeder keeps three kinds of plants:

Plant typeGenotypeFlower color
True-breeding purplePPPurple
Hybrid purplePpPurple
WhiteppWhite

The breeder transfers pollen from one plant to another by hand so that she knows exactly which two plants are the parents of each batch of seeds. She then grows the seeds and records the flower color of each offspring plant.

stimuli.title: A Single Change in a Gene
stimuli.html:
Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The instructions for one part of hemoglobin are found in a gene on chromosome 11. In most people, one three-base group in this gene reads GAG. In the sickle cell allele, the middle base has been replaced, so the group reads GTG instead. This single change causes one amino acid in the protein to be different.

That small difference matters. When oxygen levels are low, the changed hemoglobin molecules stick together into long fibers. The fibers bend red blood cells into a stiff, curved “sickle” shape. Sickled cells can block small blood vessels, causing pain and organ damage, and they break down faster than normal cells.

The sickle cell allele is recessive for the disease. A person with two copies of the allele has sickle cell disease. A person with one copy is a carrier. Carriers usually have no symptoms, and studies have shown that carriers are less likely to become seriously ill from malaria, a disease spread by mosquitoes in parts of Africa, Asia, and South America. This protection helps explain why the allele is more common in regions where malaria has long been widespread.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship among DNA, genes, and chromosomes?
options: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule that contains many genes.
A gene is a long DNA molecule that contains many chromosomes.
DNA is made of many chromosomes joined end to end.
A chromosome is a small section of one gene.
items.hint: Think of the size ladder: base, gene, chromosome.
items.explain:
A chromosome is one long, coiled DNA molecule, and a gene is a section of that DNA. So one chromosome carries many genes.

The second option reverses the relationship: genes are parts of chromosomes, not the other way around. The last two options also put the pieces in the wrong order of size.

items.prompt: One strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence A T G C C A. Which sequence is found on the complementary strand?
options: T A C G G T
A T G C C A
G C A T T G
C G T A A C
items.hint: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.
items.explain:
Pair each base in order:

A → T
T → A
G → C
C → G
C → G
A → T

Complementary strand: T A C G G T.

The sequence G C A T T G comes from pairing A with G and T with C, which is the wrong rule. A T G C C A just repeats the original strand.

items.prompt: What is the phenotype of a hybrid pea plant with genotype Pp?
options: Purple flowers
White flowers
Pale purple flowers
Some purple flowers and some white flowers
items.hint: Which allele shows its trait whenever it is present?
items.explain:
The phenotype is the trait you can see. The plant has one P allele and one p allele. Because P (purple) is dominant, it shows whenever it is present, so the plant has purple flowers, exactly like a PP plant. The table in the passage confirms this.

Pale purple would be a blend, which happens only with incomplete dominance; the passage says purple is dominant, so there is no blending.

items.prompt: Sort each genotype into the correct category.
items.hint: Homozygous means the two letters are identical, including whether they are capital or lowercase.
items.explain:
• Homozygous dominant (two capital letters): TT, AA.
  • Heterozygous (one capital and one lowercase): Pp, Gg.
  • Homozygous recessive (two lowercase letters): rr, bb.

A common error is to call Pp or Gg homozygous because both letters are the same letter of the alphabet. They are different alleles, so these genotypes are heterozygous.

items.prompt: The breeder crosses two hybrid purple plants (Pp × Pp). What is the probability that an offspring plant will have white flowers?
items.hint: Draw a Punnett square with P and p across the top and P and p down the side.
items.explain:
Pp
PPPPp
pPppp

White flowers require pp. Only 1 of the 4 boxes is pp.

1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 = 25%

75% is the probability of purple flowers (PP, Pp, Pp), so it answers the opposite question.

items.prompt: The breeder crosses a hybrid purple plant (Pp) with a white plant (pp) and grows 90 offspring plants. How many of the offspring are expected to have white flowers? Enter a whole number.
items.hint: Find the probability of pp with a Punnett square, then multiply by 90.
items.explain:
Pp
pPppp
pPppp

White (pp): 2 of 4 boxes = 2/4 = 1/2.

Expected number = 1/2 × 90 = 45 plants.

Entering 22.5 (1/4 of 90) uses the probability from a Pp × Pp cross, not this cross.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about a cross between a true-breeding purple plant (PP) and a white plant (pp).

{{0}} of the offspring will have the genotype {{1}}, so every offspring will have {{2}} flowers.

options: homozygous dominant (PP)
heterozygous (Pp)
homozygous recessive (pp)
purple
white
pale purple

items.hint: The PP parent can pass on only P. The pp parent can pass on only p.
items.explain:
PP
pPpPp
pPpPp

All 4 boxes are Pp, so 100% of the offspring are heterozygous (Pp). Because P is dominant, they all have purple flowers.

Choosing white or pale purple ignores the fact that one dominant P allele is enough to make the flowers purple.

items.prompt: Based on the results of Cross 2, which are the most likely genotypes of the two black parents?
options: Both parents are heterozygous (Bb).
Both parents are homozygous dominant (BB).
One parent is homozygous dominant (BB), and the other is heterozygous (Bb).
One parent is heterozygous (Bb), and the other is homozygous recessive (bb).
items.hint: What genotype does a white offspring have? Where did each of its alleles come from?
items.explain:
Each white offspring is bb, so it received one b allele from each parent. Both parents are black, so each also has a B allele. That makes both parents Bb.

Check with the numbers: a Bb × Bb cross is expected to give 3/4 black and 1/4 white. Total offspring = 31 + 9 = 40. Expected black = 3/4 × 40 = 30; expected white = 1/4 × 40 = 10. The actual 31 : 9 is very close.

If either parent were BB, every offspring would get at least one B and be black, so no white offspring could appear. A bb parent would be white, but both parents in Cross 2 are black.

items.prompt: Which type of mutation produces the sickle cell allele?
options: A substitution, because one base is replaced by a different base
An insertion, because an extra base is added to the gene
A deletion, because one base is removed from the gene
A chromosome loss, because all of chromosome 11 is missing
items.hint: Compare GAG with GTG. How many bases are in each? What changed?
items.explain:
The normal group is GAG and the sickle cell group is GTG. Both have three bases; the middle base A was replaced by T. One base swapped for another is a substitution.

An insertion would make the sequence longer and a deletion would make it shorter, but the length did not change. The passage says the gene is on chromosome 11, so the chromosome is present, not lost.

items.prompt: Two parents are both carriers of the sickle cell allele. What is the probability that their next child will also be a carrier? Enter your answer as a percent.
items.hint: Use S for the normal allele and s for the sickle cell allele. Carriers are Ss. Which boxes in Ss × Ss are carriers?
items.explain:
Carriers have one normal allele and one sickle cell allele: Ss × Ss.

Ss
SSSSs
sSsss

Carrier (Ss): 2 of 4 boxes.

2 ÷ 4 = 0.50 = 50%

25% is the chance of sickle cell disease (ss), not the chance of being a carrier. 75% is the chance of not having the disease (SS or Ss).

items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
options: Changing a single base in a gene can change the protein the gene codes for.
Two parents who do not have sickle cell disease can have a child who has the disease.
Every mutation is harmful to the person who carries it.
A person with one copy of the sickle cell allele has sickle cell disease.
The sickle cell mutation adds an extra chromosome to each red blood cell.
items.hint: Check each statement against the passage. Watch for words like “every” and for statements about carriers.
items.explain:
• Supported: One base change (GAG to GTG) changes one amino acid in hemoglobin, which changes how the protein behaves.
  • Supported: Carriers usually have no symptoms. Two carriers can each pass on the recessive allele, giving a child with two copies and the disease.
  • Not supported: carriers are protected against severe malaria, so this mutation can be helpful in some settings. The passage contradicts “every mutation is harmful.”
  • Not supported: one copy makes a person a carrier; the disease requires two copies.
  • Not supported: the mutation is a change in one base, not an extra chromosome.

items.prompt: In snapdragon plants, flower color shows incomplete dominance. Plants with genotype RR have red flowers, plants with genotype WW have white flowers, and plants with genotype RW have pink flowers. A gardener crosses two pink-flowered plants and grows 200 seedlings. How many seedlings are expected to have pink flowers?
items.hint: Draw an RW × RW Punnett square. Which genotype gives pink flowers?
items.explain:
RW
RRRRW
WRWWW

Phenotypes: 1 red (RR) : 2 pink (RW) : 1 white (WW).

Probability of pink = 2/4 = 1/2.

Expected pink = 1/2 × 200 = 100 seedlings.

150 is the result if you treat red as fully dominant (3/4 × 200), but with incomplete dominance the RR plants are red, not pink. 50 is the expected number of red (or of white) seedlings.
